subject: chemistry
topicDisplay: Reactivity 2.2 & 2.3 — rate and extent of reaction
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Measuring the rate of a reaction
What changes the rate, and why
Activation energy and the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution
Dynamic equilibrium in a closed system
What the size of K means, and what changes it

questions.q: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g). Which quantity is the rate of this reaction at a particular moment?
options: The total time taken for all of the H₂O₂ in the sample to decompose
The total volume of O₂ given off by the time the reaction has stopped
The decrease in the concentration of H₂O₂ per unit time at that moment
The concentration of H₂O₂ at that moment divided by the time elapsed so far
optionWhy: A student who treats rate and time as the same thing picks this. Time taken is not a rate; a reaction that takes longer has a smaller rate. A rate is a change divided by a time.
A student who confuses how fast with how much picks this. The total volume of O₂ depends on the amount of H₂O₂ used, not on how quickly it decomposes, and it is not divided by any time.

Rate is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time, in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. At a particular moment it is the gradient of the tangent to the concentration–time curve, quoted as a positive value for the decrease in [H₂O₂].

A student who divides the y-value by the x-value picks this. The rate is a change in concentration per unit time; [H₂O₂]/t is not even an average rate, and the rate at an instant needs the gradient of the tangent.
questions.explain: Rate is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time, in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. At a particular moment it is the gradient of the tangent to the concentration–time curve, quoted as a positive value for the decrease in [H₂O₂].

questions.q: Magnesium ribbon reacts with excess hydrochloric acid, and the hydrogen is collected in a gas syringe. A graph of the volume of hydrogen (y-axis, cm³) against time (x-axis, s) is a curve that is steep at first, becomes less steep and levels off at 60 cm³ at 100 s. The curve passes through the point (20 s, 34 cm³). A tangent drawn to the curve at t = 20 s passes through the points (0 s, 10 cm³) and (40 s, 58 cm³). What is the rate of reaction at t = 20 s?
options: 1.70 cm³ s⁻¹
0.60 cm³ s⁻¹
0.83 cm³ s⁻¹
1.20 cm³ s⁻¹
optionWhy: A student who divides the coordinates of the point gets 34 cm³ ÷ 20 s = 1.70 cm³ s⁻¹. That is the average rate over the first 20 s, which is larger than the rate at 20 s because the reaction has been slowing down. Use the tangent: 48 cm³ ÷ 40 s = 1.20 cm³ s⁻¹.

A student who assumes the rate is the same throughout divides the final volume by the total time: 60 cm³ ÷ 100 s = 0.60 cm³ s⁻¹. That is the average over the whole reaction; the rate at 20 s is the tangent's gradient, 1.20 cm³ s⁻¹.
A student who calculates the gradient upside down gets 40 s ÷ 48 cm³ = 0.83 (in s cm⁻³, which is not a rate unit). Gradient = Δy/Δx = 48 cm³ ÷ 40 s = 1.20 cm³ s⁻¹.
The rate at 20 s is the gradient of the tangent: (58 − 10) cm³ ÷ (40 − 0) s = 48 cm³ ÷ 40 s = 1.20 cm³ s⁻¹.
questions.explain: The rate at 20 s is the gradient of the tangent: (58 − 10) cm³ ÷ (40 − 0) s = 48 cm³ ÷ 40 s = 1.20 cm³ s⁻¹.
questions.working: Gradient of the tangent at t = 20 s = Δ(volume)/Δ(time) = (58 cm³ − 10 cm³)/(40 s − 0 s) = 48 cm³/40 s = 1.20 cm³ s⁻¹.

questions.q: Two reactant molecules in a gas collide with a combined kinetic energy greater than the activation energy, Ea, of the reaction, but they do not react. Which statement explains this?
options: No catalyst was present, and a reaction cannot take place at all without one.
They collided with an orientation that did not bring the reacting atoms together.
Their combined energy was less than the size of the enthalpy change of reaction, ΔH.
No spark or heating had first supplied the activation energy to start the reaction.
optionWhy: A student who thinks reactions need a catalyst picks this. A catalyst only provides a faster pathway; without one, collisions with E ≥ Ea and a proper orientation still react.

A successful collision needs both energy equal to or greater than Ea and a proper orientation. With enough energy but the wrong collision geometry, the atoms that must bond do not meet, so no reaction occurs.
A student who confuses Ea with ΔH picks this. The energy a collision needs is Ea, the minimum energy for reaction; ΔH is the energy difference between reactants and products and is not the threshold.

A student who thinks activation energy is a one-off 'start-up' energy from a spark or flame picks this. Ea is the minimum energy each colliding pair must have, and this collision already had more than Ea, so no outside energy was missing. The collision failed because of its orientation.
questions.explain: A successful collision needs both energy equal to or greater than Ea and a proper orientation. With enough energy but the wrong collision geometry, the atoms that must bond do not meet, so no reaction occurs.

questions.q: Two experiments use equal masses of calcium carbonate and the same volume of excess hydrochloric acid of the same concentration at the same temperature. In experiment 1 the calcium carbonate is a single lump; in experiment 2 it is a fine powder. Which statement is correct?
options: The powder reacts faster, as more of its particles are exposed, so collisions with acid are more frequent.
The lump reacts faster, as its greater size gives it the larger surface area for the acid particles to attack.
The powder reacts faster, as its exposed particles collide with the acid particles with more energy.
The powder gives off more carbon dioxide in total, as its faster reaction goes further to completion.
optionWhy: The powder has a much larger total surface area than the lump of the same mass, so more calcium carbonate particles can be hit by acid particles. Collisions are more frequent, so there are more successful collisions per second.
A student who compares one lump with one grain picks this. For equal masses, breaking the solid up exposes far more surface in total, so the powder has the larger surface area and reacts faster.

A student who thinks surface area changes collision energy picks this. The energies of collisions depend on temperature, which is the same; the powder reacts faster because collisions are more frequent.

A student who links a faster reaction with more product picks this. The masses of calcium carbonate are equal and the acid is in excess, so both give the same volume of CO₂; the powder simply gives it off sooner.
questions.explain: The powder has a much larger total surface area than the lump of the same mass, so more calcium carbonate particles can be hit by acid particles. Collisions are more frequent, so there are more successful collisions per second.

questions.q: Hydrogen iodide decomposes: 2HI(g) → H₂(g) + I₂(g). A sample of hydrogen iodide is compressed to half its volume at constant temperature. What is the effect on the rate of reaction, and why?
options: It is unchanged: there are equal amounts of gas on both sides of the equation, so pressure has no effect.
It increases: the compressed molecules collide more energetically, so more collisions exceed Ea.
It increases: a larger amount of H₂ and I₂ can now form from the same amount of HI as before.
It increases: collisions become more frequent, and the fraction with E ≥ Ea is unchanged.
optionWhy: A student who applies Le Châtelier's principle to rates picks this. Equal amounts of gas on each side matter for an equilibrium position, not for the rate. Compressing the gas increases the concentration of HI, so the rate increases.

A student who thinks crowding makes collisions harder picks this. At constant temperature the energy distribution is unchanged; compression increases how often molecules collide, not how energetically.

A student who links a faster rate with more product picks this. The amount of HI is unchanged, so compressing it does not change the amount of H₂ and I₂ that can form; it changes how quickly they form.

Halving the volume doubles the concentration of HI molecules, so they collide more often. The temperature, and so the fraction of collisions with E ≥ Ea, is unchanged; more collisions per second means more successful collisions per second.
questions.explain: Halving the volume doubles the concentration of HI molecules, so they collide more often. The temperature, and so the fraction of collisions with E ≥ Ea, is unchanged; more collisions per second means more successful collisions per second.

questions.q: A Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution is plotted for a sample of gas at 300 K, with number of particles on the y-axis and kinetic energy on the x-axis. The curve starts at the origin, rises to a peak and falls to a long tail that approaches the energy axis. Which describes the curve for the same sample at 400 K?
options: The peak is higher and at a higher energy, as more particles move fast, and the area is larger.
The whole curve moves to higher energy by the same amount, keeping its shape and height.
The peak is lower and at a higher energy, the tail is higher, and the area under the curve is unchanged.
The curve is unchanged, but the activation energy becomes lower, so more particles exceed it.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a higher temperature gives 'more' of everything picks this. The area represents the number of particles, which does not change; because the distribution spreads out, the peak must be lower.
A student who thinks every particle gains the same energy picks this. The distribution changes shape: it becomes flatter and broader, with the peak lower and at a higher energy.

The number of particles is unchanged, so the area under the curve is the same. At the higher temperature the energies spread out to higher values, so the curve is flatter: the peak is lower and moves to the right, and more particles are in the high-energy tail.
A student who thinks heating lowers Ea picks this. Ea is fixed for the pathway; it is the curve that changes with temperature, so that a larger area lies beyond the same Ea.
questions.explain: The number of particles is unchanged, so the area under the curve is the same. At the higher temperature the energies spread out to higher values, so the curve is flatter: the peak is lower and moves to the right, and more particles are in the high-energy tail.

questions.q: The graph shows Maxwell–Boltzmann energy distributions, P and Q, for the same sample of a gas at two different temperatures. The activation energy, Ea, of a reaction of the gas is marked. Which statement is correct?
options: P is at the higher temperature, because its higher peak shows more of its particles have energy above Ea.
Q is at the higher temperature, because every one of its particles has more energy than any particle in P.
Q is at the higher temperature, and more of its particles have energies of at least Ea.
Q is at the higher temperature, which lowers Ea for Q, so more of its particles can react.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the hotter curve has the higher peak picks this. The area under each curve is the same (same number of particles), so the hotter sample, spread over more energies, must have the lower peak. P's high peak lies at low energy; beyond Ea it is Q that has the larger area.

A student who thinks heating gives every particle the same extra energy picks this. The curves overlap: Q still has many low-energy particles and P has some high-energy ones. Heating changes the shape of the distribution, increasing the fraction of particles above Ea, not every particle's energy.

At a higher temperature the distribution flattens and spreads to higher energies, so the hotter sample has the lower, broader peak: that is Q. Beyond the Ea line the area under Q is larger than under P, so a larger fraction of Q's particles have energy of at least Ea and a larger fraction of collisions can react.

A student who thinks heating lowers the activation energy picks this. Ea is fixed by the reaction pathway, so the one Ea line applies to both samples; what changes with temperature is the fraction of particles whose energy is at least Ea.
questions.explain: At a higher temperature the distribution flattens and spreads to higher energies, so the hotter sample has the lower, broader peak: that is Q. Beyond the Ea line the area under Q is larger than under P, so a larger fraction of Q's particles have energy of at least Ea and a larger fraction of collisions can react.

figure.alt: Maxwell–Boltzmann graph: number of particles (vertical axis) against kinetic energy (horizontal axis), no numbers. Curve P rises steeply from the origin to a high, narrow peak at low energy and falls quickly. Curve Q rises more gradually to a lower, broader peak further along the energy axis and falls more slowly, so its tail lies above P's at high energies; the two curves cross once. A vertical dashed line labelled Ea is drawn far to the right of both peaks, in the tail region.

questions.q: Catalase is an enzyme that catalyses the exothermic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide: 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g). The energy profile of the uncatalysed reaction rises from the reactants to a maximum and falls to products that are lower in energy than the reactants. How does the profile differ when catalase is present?
options: The maximum is lower and the products are lower in energy, so the reaction becomes more exothermic.
The maximum is lower, while the energies of the reactants and products, and so ΔH, are unchanged.
The reactants are raised to a higher energy, closer to the top of an unchanged maximum.
The forward Ea is lower but the reverse Ea is unchanged, as only the forward reaction speeds up.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a catalyst lowers the whole profile picks this. The products are the same substances with the same energy, so ΔH is unchanged; only the maximum is lower.

An enzyme is a biological catalyst: it provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy. It does not change the energies of the reactants or products, so the profile starts and ends at the same energies and ΔH is unchanged.
A student who thinks a catalyst gives particles energy picks this. Catalase does not add energy to the reactants; it lowers the maximum by providing a different pathway.
A student who thinks a catalyst affects only the forward reaction picks this. Lowering the maximum lowers the forward and reverse activation energies by the same amount, so ΔH stays the same.
questions.explain: An enzyme is a biological catalyst: it provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy. It does not change the energies of the reactants or products, so the profile starts and ends at the same energies and ΔH is unchanged.

questions.q: The diagram shows the energy profile of an exothermic reaction without a catalyst (solid line) and with a catalyst (dashed line). Which arrow represents the activation energy of the catalysed reverse reaction?
options: Arrow Y
Arrow W
Arrow X
Arrow Z
optionWhy: A student who thinks a catalyst lowers only the forward activation energy picks this. The catalysed pathway has one lower maximum that both directions pass over, so the reverse activation energy is also lowered: it is Z, from the products to the catalysed maximum. Y is the uncatalysed reverse activation energy.

A student who measures every activation energy from the reactants picks this. W is the activation energy of the catalysed forward reaction. The reverse reaction starts from the products, so its activation energy is measured from the products level: Z.

A student who confuses activation energy with ΔH picks this. X is the energy difference between reactants and products, ΔH, which the catalyst does not change. The activation energy of the catalysed reverse reaction is the rise from the products to the catalysed maximum, Z.

The reverse reaction starts from the products, and with the catalyst present it passes over the lower, catalysed maximum. Its activation energy is the rise from the products level to that maximum, which is Z.
questions.explain: The reverse reaction starts from the products, and with the catalyst present it passes over the lower, catalysed maximum. Its activation energy is the rise from the products level to that maximum, which is Z.

questions.q:
Hydrogen and iodine are heated in a sealed flask at constant temperature until the amount of hydrogen iodide no longer changes:
H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)
Which statement must be true of the mixture at this point?
options: No HI forms or decomposes now, as both reactions have stopped.
HI forms and decomposes at equal rates, so its amount stays the same.
The concentrations of H₂, I₂ and HI have become equal to each other.
Half of the hydrogen and iodine has been converted into hydrogen iodide.
optionWhy: A student who thinks equilibrium is a state of rest picks this. The concentrations are constant because the forward and backward reactions occur at equal rates, not because they have stopped.

The system is in dynamic equilibrium: in the closed flask the forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates, so the concentrations of H₂, I₂ and HI are constant although the reactions have not stopped.

A student who reads 'equilibrium' as 'equal amounts' picks this. It is the rates of the two reactions that are equal; the concentrations are constant but their values depend on K and the starting amounts.

A student who pictures equilibrium as the halfway point of a reaction picks this. How far the reaction goes is set by K at that temperature, not by a halfway rule; nothing in the stem says half has reacted.
questions.explain: The system is in dynamic equilibrium: in the closed flask the forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates, so the concentrations of H₂, I₂ and HI are constant although the reactions have not stopped.

questions.q: Some liquid bromine is placed in a flask, which is then stoppered and kept at constant temperature. The brown colour of the vapour above the liquid deepens at first and then stays constant. Which statement about the flask once the colour is constant is correct?
options: Bromine still evaporates and condenses, and the two processes occur at equal rates.
Bromine has stopped evaporating, because the vapour above the liquid is saturated.
The system cannot be at equilibrium, because no chemical reaction takes place.
The concentration of Br₂ is now the same in the liquid and in the vapour.
optionWhy: This is a dynamic physical equilibrium in a closed system: molecules leave the liquid and return to it at equal rates, so the amount of vapour, and hence the colour, stays constant.

A student who thinks nothing happens at equilibrium picks this. The vapour is saturated in the sense that its pressure is constant, but evaporation continues; it is balanced by condensation at the same rate.
A student who thinks equilibrium applies only to chemical reactions picks this. A change of state in a closed container reaches a dynamic equilibrium with the same characteristics as a chemical one.

A student who believes that concentrations become equal at equilibrium picks this. The liquid is far more concentrated than the vapour; at equilibrium the rates of evaporation and condensation are equal, not the concentrations.
questions.explain: This is a dynamic physical equilibrium in a closed system: molecules leave the liquid and return to it at equal rates, so the amount of vapour, and hence the colour, stays constant.

questions.q:
Which is the equilibrium constant expression for the following reaction?
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)
options: K = [N₂][H₂]³/[NH₃]²
K = [NH₃]²/([N₂][H₂]³)
K = [NH₃]²/([N₂]+[H₂]³)
optionWhy: A student who multiplies each concentration by its coefficient picks this. The coefficients become powers, not multipliers: 2NH₃ gives [NH₃]² and 3H₂ gives [H₂]³.
A student who puts the reactants on top picks this. This is the expression for the reverse reaction, 2NH₃(g) ⇌ N₂(g) + 3H₂(g), whose value is 1/K.
Products over reactants, with each concentration raised to the power of its coefficient in the equation: [NH₃]² on top, [N₂] and [H₂]³ multiplied together on the bottom.
A student who carries the '+' sign of the equation into the expression picks this. The reactant terms are multiplied, not added: the denominator is [N₂][H₂]³.
questions.explain: Products over reactants, with each concentration raised to the power of its coefficient in the equation: [NH₃]² on top, [N₂] and [H₂]³ multiplied together on the bottom.

questions.q: For the reaction A(g) ⇌ B(g), K = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ at 298 K. Which statement about this reaction at 298 K is correct?
options: At equilibrium, the mixture consists almost entirely of A.
At equilibrium, A and B are present in similar amounts.
The small value of K shows that equilibrium is reached slowly.
Adding a catalyst would increase the equilibrium yield of B.
optionWhy: K ≪ 1, so [B]/[A] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ at equilibrium: the position of equilibrium lies far to the left and very little A is converted into B.
A student who expects every equilibrium to lie roughly halfway picks this. Similar amounts would correspond to K close to 1; here [B]/[A] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸.
A student who links the size of K with rate picks this. K describes how far the reaction goes, not how fast; a reaction with a small K may reach equilibrium quickly or slowly.

A student who thinks a catalyst shifts the equilibrium picks this. A catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions by the same factor, so equilibrium is reached sooner, but K and the equilibrium composition are unchanged.
questions.explain: K ≪ 1, so [B]/[A] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ at equilibrium: the position of equilibrium lies far to the left and very little A is converted into B.

questions.q: For the reaction X(g) ⇌ Y(g), K = 1.0 × 10¹⁵ at 298 K. Which statement about this reaction at 298 K is correct?
options: At equilibrium, the mixture is made up almost entirely of X.
At equilibrium, almost all of X has been converted into Y.
At equilibrium, X and Y are present in similar amounts.
The large value of K shows that equilibrium is reached quickly.
optionWhy: A student who puts the reactants on top of the expression reads K as [X]/[Y] and so thinks a large K means mostly X. K = [Y]/[X], so a large K means mostly Y.
K ≫ 1, so [Y]/[X] = 1.0 × 10¹⁵ at equilibrium: the position of equilibrium lies far to the right and the reaction goes almost to completion.
A student who expects every equilibrium to lie roughly halfway picks this. Similar amounts would correspond to K close to 1; here [Y]/[X] = 1.0 × 10¹⁵.
A student who links the size of K with rate picks this. K describes how far the reaction goes, not how fast; a reaction with a very large K may still be extremely slow.
questions.explain: K ≫ 1, so [Y]/[X] = 1.0 × 10¹⁵ at equilibrium: the position of equilibrium lies far to the right and the reaction goes almost to completion.

questions.q:
The forward reaction in the following equilibrium is exothermic:
2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g)
The temperature of the equilibrium mixture is increased at constant pressure. How do the amount of SO₃ and the value of K at the new equilibrium compare with those at the original equilibrium?
options: A larger amount of SO₃ and a larger value of K.
A smaller amount of SO₃ and a smaller value of K.
An unchanged amount of SO₃ and an unchanged K.
A smaller amount of SO₃ and the same value of K.
optionWhy: A student who thinks heating makes every reaction go further picks this. Heating favours the endothermic (backward) direction, so less SO₃ forms and K decreases.

Raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction, here the backward reaction, so less SO₃ is present at the new equilibrium; K depends on temperature and, for an exothermic forward reaction, decreases.

A student who treats temperature like a catalyst, speeding up both directions equally, picks this. The endothermic (backward) rate increases more, so the equilibrium shifts to the left and K decreases.

A student who applies Le Châtelier’s principle correctly but thinks K is constant at every temperature picks this. K is constant only at a fixed temperature; the shift to the left caused by heating is accompanied by a smaller K.
questions.explain: Raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction, here the backward reaction, so less SO₃ is present at the new equilibrium; K depends on temperature and, for an exothermic forward reaction, decreases.
